conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postpartum/Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a brief, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team, and our only goal today is to make sure you feel safe, heard, and supported.

We’ll go through each question one at a time, focusing on the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. Ready to begin?

Question 1: Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
Mostly it’s felt difficult... I do laugh once in a while, like when my sister sent a silly video, but even then it fades fast and I go back to feeling flat. Humor just doesn’t come easily anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
No, not really. I laughed maybe once this week, and it felt forced. Mostly I’m too tired or low to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really... I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but this week nothing sounds worth the effort. I still go through the motions, but it’s more “I should” than “I want to.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot of the time. If the baby won’t settle or I can’t get the swaddle right, I keep thinking I must be doing something wrong, that a “good mom” would figure it out. Even little things—like spilling a bottle—turn into this loop of “I’m failing him.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, pretty much all the time. My mind keeps racing with “what-ifs”—what if he stops breathing, what if I miss a cue, what if I’m not producing enough milk—so even when everything’s calm, my chest feels tight and I can’t settle.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes. I’ll be rocking the baby in the quiet and suddenly my heart’s racing and I feel like I can’t catch my breath, even though nothing’s happening. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary while it’s going on.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, quite often. Between feedings, the crying, the house a mess, and trying to sleep, it feels like I’m drowning a little. Some mornings I just lie there staring at the ceiling, thinking I’ll never catch up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—replaying every little thing I did wrong that day, worrying about the baby, worrying I’m a lousy mom. It takes forever to fall asleep, and when I do, I jolt awake at every tiny sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes, most of the time. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. Even when I’m holding the baby, I’ll just start tearing up for no clear reason and can’t shake the sadness.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, quite a lot. It’s happened a few times this week—once while folding laundry, another time while trying to get him to latch. The tears just come and I can’t seem to stop them, even when I tell myself I should be happy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

It sounds like you've been carrying a very heavy emotional load since your baby arrived. You described laughter feeling forced, daily activities losing their sparkle, and a persistent gray cloud of sadness that even cuddling your little one can't seem to lift. You shared how worries race through your mind at all hours, making rest elusive, and how everyday hiccups-like a spilled bottle-spiral into harsh self-blame. These feelings, while painful and exhausting, are important signals, and reaching out today shows real strength.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no laughter this week and describes it as forced, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, consistent with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a lot of the time," equating normal infant-care challenges with personal failure, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-constant, intrusive 'what-if' worries and physical tension, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly says "Sometimes" and describes sudden episodes of racing heart and breathlessness with no trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and feeling like "drowning," indicating intermittent coping difficulties matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts and prolonged sleep-onset difficulty most of the time, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness, frequent crying, and inability to shake the feeling, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent crying episodes ('quite a lot,' 'a few times this week'), matching 'Yes, quite often'.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 24 falls well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression. The patient endorsed severe loss of enjoyment and laughter (Q1-2), near-constant self-reproach (Q3), prominent free-floating anxiety and panic (Q4-5), nightly sleep disruption driven by rumination (Q7), and frequent crying spells (Q8-9). These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness, and insomnia. No self-harm ideation was reported (Q10). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Enlist practical help-partner, family, or postpartum doula-for night feeds and household tasks so you can rest
4. Practice 5-minute breathing breaks when panic surges; place baby in safe spot, inhale 4s, exhale 6s
5. Keep lights low and screens off during night feeds to protect melatonin and improve sleep efficiency
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track changes after treatment starts
7. Carry emergency contacts: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and your local <med>postpartum support</med> warmline
8. Lean on peer supports-<med>Postpartum Support International</med> groups or trusted moms-so you feel less alone
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale (self-report)

Symptom Endorsement  
- Marked anhedonia: minimal laughter, no anticipatory enjoyment  
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” frequent crying spells (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame over routine infant care (Q3)  
- Chronic anxiety, intrusive “what-ifs,” physical tension (Q4)  
- Panicky episodes with autonomic symptoms (Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm / “drowning” sensation (Q6)  
- Sleep initiation difficulty linked to ruminative worry (Q7)

Pattern  
All nine mood/anxiety items endorsed at clinically significant level; functioning clearly impaired.  
Self-harm item denied (Q10).

Screening Significance  
High likelihood of major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features in postpartum period. No acute safety concern per self-report.

Next Step  
Recommend formal diagnostic interview (DSM-5-TR) and discussion of evidence-based treatment options at follow-up.
